To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ethanol-induced cytotoxic effects on cranial neural crest cells in culture may be mediated, at least partly, through free radical generation.

1) ethanol exposure results in the production of free radicals by neural crest cells, 2) free radicals produced by the NCCs are cytotoxic, 3) ethanol exposure results is cytotoxicity, 4) the ethanol-induced cytotoxic effects on NCCs are ameliorated by antioxidants, 5) the cytotoxic effects of exogenous free radical production are also ameliorated by free radical scavengers, and 6) the cytotoxicity produced by ethanol exposure

ethanol-induced NCC damage is associated with increased free radical generation, and that the free radical scavengers, superoxide dismutate, catalase, and alpha-tocopheral, ameliorate the ethanol-induced cytotoxic effects on NCCs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms of free radical-induced neural crest cell (ncc) death and its relationship to ethanol toxicity.
the role of free radical damage in ethanol-induced NCE death.
the effects of ethanol on the development of the cranial neural crest.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NCCs are very sensitive to free radicals, and the sensitivity to ethanol-induced free radicals may be the reason why they are vulnerable to ethanol-induced damage.
ethanol-induced NCC damage in mammalian fetuses results, in part, from free radical generation and subsequent cytotoxicity.

ethanol exposure results in the generation of free radical species, which are toxic to NCCs, and that this mechanism may be responsible for ethanol-induced NCC damage and the craniofacial malformations observed in human fetal-alcohol syndrome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the free radical scavengers significantly ameliorated the ethanol- and xanthine/xanthen oxidase-induced cytotoxicity.
ethanol induces free radicals in the neural crest and that these free radicals are responsible for the neural crest cell death.
the free radical theory of aging is applicable to the aging process in neural crest cells and the free radical theory may be applicable to ethanol-induced neural crest damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ethanol-induced cranial NCC damage in mammals may result, at leas in part, from free radical-mediated cytotoxicity.
ethanol is a potent free radical generator and that ethanol-induced NCC cytotoxic effects can be ameliorated with the addition of free radical scavengers.
ethanol exposure causes free radical generation in NCCs, which in turn causes cytotoxic effects.
